added_lemmas.statement:
For every \(0<\alpha\le 1/4\),
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le 5\min\{1,\omega_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\]
The bound is attained by a deterministic observed-data interval and therefore remains valid when the competing class permits randomization by the independent external randomizer \(R\).  In addition, if \(x_\alpha<\sum_{l=1}^Lq_l\) and no coordinate of the water-filling optimizer is capped, meaning \(\lambda_\alpha w_l/q_l<1\) for every \(l\), then
\[
 \omega_\alpha(w,q)=\sqrt{Sx_\alpha}
 =\sqrt{S\log(1/\alpha)}.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix \(0<\alpha\le1/4\).  By \(\mathrm{thm{:}trimmed\text{-}upper}\), there is a deterministic interval \(I_J(D)\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\) whose pointwise length, for every fixed potential-outcome schedule in \(\mathcal M_n(B)\), is at most
\[
 2\min\{1,\rho_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\tag{1}
\]
Because the infimum in \(\mathrm{def{:}length\text{-}risk}\) ranges over a class that contains this deterministic rule, taking first the expectation, then the supremum over fixed schedules, and finally the infimum over all rules gives
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le 2\min\{1,\rho_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\tag{2}
\]
The strengthened trimming duality in \(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\) gives
\[
 \rho_\alpha(w,q)\le\frac52\omega_\alpha(w,q).
\tag{3}
\]
For every \(u\ge0\) and every \(K\ge1\),
\[
 \min\{1,Ku\}\le K\min\{1,u\}.
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, if \(u\le1\), the left side is at most \(Ku\), and if \(u>1\), it is at most \(1\le K\).  Combining (2)--(4) with \(K=5/2\) proves
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le5\min\{1,\omega_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\tag{5}
\]
This comparison uses a deterministic member of \(\mathfrak C_\alpha\); enlarging the decision class to procedures depending measurably on the independent \(R\) cannot invalidate the upper bound.

It remains to verify the no-cap formula.  Put \(x=x_\alpha\).  Under \(x<\sum_lq_l\), the definition of the water-filling multiplier and its optimality certificate in \(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\) give
\[
 \delta_l^*=\min\{1,\lambda_\alpha w_l/q_l\},
 \qquad
 \sum_lq_l(\delta_l^*)^2=x.
\tag{6}
\]
The asserted no-cap condition turns (6) into \(\delta_l^*=\lambda_\alpha w_l/q_l\) for every \(l\).  Since \(q_l>0\), \(w_l>0\), and
\(S=\sum_lw_l^2/q_l>0\), the constraint in (6) becomes
\[
 x=\lambda_\alpha^2\sum_l\frac{w_l^2}{q_l}
  =\lambda_\alpha^2S,
 \qquad
 \lambda_\alpha=\sqrt{x/S}.
\tag{7}
\]
Substitution into the objective of \(\mathrm{def{:}capped\text{-}modulus}\) yields
\[
 \omega_\alpha(w,q)
 =\sum_lw_l\delta_l^*
 =\lambda_\alpha\sum_l\frac{w_l^2}{q_l}
 =\lambda_\alpha S
 =\sqrt{Sx}.
\tag{8}
\]
As \(x=x_\alpha=\log(1/\alpha)\), (8) is the claimed identity.
added_lemmas.justification: The deterministic trimmed interval and the sharpened trimming dual give the explicit unrestricted factor-five upper bound, while the active uncapped constraint gives the exact quadratic formula.
added_lemmas.gap: The matching universal linear lower bound for all measurable externally randomized intervals remains open.
added_lemmas.consumer: The residual water-filling question can now be stated solely as a lower-bound problem.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
Determine whether there is a universal constant \(c>0\) such that, for every \(0<\alpha\le1/4\) and every unequal-clique design in the model class,
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \ge c\min\{1,\omega_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\]
The lower bound must hold when the infimum defining \(\mathcal R_\alpha\) ranges over every measurable interval procedure, including procedures randomized by the independent external randomizer \(R\).  This universal linear lower bound is the sole residual question.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The original question also asks for an optimizer certificate, trimming duality, an unrestricted upper bound, and a no-cap formula. Those clauses are now proved. Retaining them as open would misstate the frontier; the universal linear lower bound is the only unresolved clause.

proposed.statement:
Determine whether there is a universal constant \(c>0\) such that, for every \(0<\alpha\le1/4\) and every unequal-clique design in the model class,
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \ge c\min\{1,\omega_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\]
The lower bound must hold when the infimum defining \(\mathcal R_\alpha\) ranges over every measurable interval procedure, including procedures randomized by the independent external randomizer \(R\).  This universal linear lower bound is the sole residual question.
proposed.justification: The capped optimizer, trimming dual, unrestricted upper bound, no-cap formula, and exact consistency boundary are proved; this question is retained solely for the matching all-measurable randomized-interval lower bound.
proposed.gap: A universal linear weighted-erasure lower bound still needs a rigorous interval-spread argument that controls compact-support boundaries, random reveal information, and external randomization.
proposed.consumer: Closing this question would sharpen the proved dominance-aware upper modulus from a one-sided guarantee to a two-sided minimax confidence-length frontier.

obligation.what_is_open: Prove the matching unrestricted minimax lower bound of linear order in the capped modulus for all measurable externally randomized intervals.
obligation.obstruction: The finite optimizer, trimming duality, and cubic common-location converse do not control posterior or concentration-function spread strongly enough to imply a linear lower bound.
obligation.attempted: The optimizer, no-cap formula, factor-five upper bound, and cubic all-procedure lower bound are closed. In accordance with the directive, no unsupported posterior-spread generalization is asserted.
obligation.partial_result:
The capped optimizer and both computable sides are closed.  The strengthened trimming duality gives
\[
 \omega_\alpha(w,q)\le\rho_\alpha(w,q)
 \le\frac52\omega_\alpha(w,q),
 \qquad
 \omega_1(w,q)\le\rho_0(w,q)\le2\omega_1(w,q).
\]
Together with the trimmed interval, \(\mathrm{thm{:}capped\text{-}modulus\text{-}upper}\) proves
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le5\min\{1,\omega_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\]
When no cap binds, the active quadratic constraint gives
\(\omega_\alpha(w,q)=\sqrt{S\log(1/\alpha)}\).  On the converse side, \(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}erasure\text{-}consistency\text{-}lower}\) proves
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \ge
 \frac{\omega_\alpha(w,q)^3}
 {128\log(1/\alpha)+8\omega_\alpha(w,q)^2}
 \ge
 \frac{\omega_\alpha(w,q)^3}{136\log(1/\alpha)}.
\]
Thus the only unresolved step is to replace this cubic converse by a universal linear converse at nonzero finite confidence.

proposed_core_edits.reason: After narrowing the question, its dependency list and metadata must refer only to the residual lower bound and the proved results that bracket it.

open_obligations.what_is_open: Prove a universal constant lower bound of linear order in the capped water-filling modulus for every measurable interval procedure, including procedures using the independent external randomizer.
open_obligations.obstruction: The proved capped perturbation and common-location no-reveal construction yield a cubic lower bound, but they do not establish the posterior interval spread or concentration-function control needed for a linear lower bound under heterogeneous moving-support erasures.
open_obligations.attempted: The KKT optimizer, strengthened trimming dual, no-cap identity, factor-five unrestricted upper bound, and cubic all-procedure converse have been completed. Per the maximality directive, the rejected posterior-spread construction was not retried or generalized.

prose_updates.tldr: Unequal clique sizes turn full-neighborhood All Treat and All Control exposure into independent nonidentical categorical reveals. The exact centered block Horvitz--Thompson increment is at most \(w_l/(2q_l)\), giving the clipped half-width \(\sqrt{S\log(2/\alpha)}+M\log(2/\alpha)/6\). Trimming is within a factor \(5/2\) of the capped water-filling modulus and yields the unrestricted upper bound \(\mathcal R_\alpha\le5\min\{1,\omega_\alpha\}\). A cubic common-location lower bound proves the exact fixed-confidence consistency boundary, and a separate product-Rademacher argument gives \(\Theta_\alpha(k^{-1/2})\) for the stated two-scale family. The sole unresolved sharp-frontier step is a universal linear weighted-erasure lower bound for all measurable externally randomized intervals. The pinned \(\texttt{szonszein/interference}\) version \(0.1.0\) diagnostic reports structural graph rejection separately from package-versus-reference exposure-label mismatch and releases the corrected interval only after both checks pass.

project_justification.gap: Existing partial-interference confidence procedures do not characterize worst-case expected length over every measurable externally randomized interval under fixed balanced Bernoulli assignment on unequal cliques. The exact consistency boundary is settled, the capped optimizer and trimming dual are certified, and the unrestricted upper bound is explicit. The sole remaining sharp-frontier gap is to strengthen the proved cubic capped-erasure converse to a universal linear lower bound.
project_justification.niche: The paper treats the known assignment distribution as the sole inferential randomness and exposes three computable design scales: the quadratic rare-exposure scale \(S\), the largest centered-increment scale \(M/2\), and the capped water-filling or trimming scale. The capped scale is necessary and sufficient for fixed-confidence consistency and controls honest length from above even when a dominant rare block makes \(S\) misleading.
project_justification.fill: The proved contribution consists of the exact independent categorical block reduction, the observed-data block Horvitz--Thompson estimator, the clipped Bernstein interval with linear term \(M\log(2/\alpha)/6\), the bias-protected trimmed interval, the certified capped water-filling optimizer, the factor-\(5/2\) trimming dual, the factor-five unrestricted upper bound, the cubic all-procedure lower bound, and the exact consistency equivalence. A dedicated product-Rademacher anti-concentration argument also proves the fixed-confidence \(\Theta_\alpha(k^{-1/2})\) rate for the specified two-scale family. The note leaves the universal linear converse open rather than promoting the special-family lower bound to the full class.

prose_updates.related_work: TchetgenTchetgenVanderWeele2012, Section 4.3, constructs Hoeffding intervals for binary allocation-strategy effects under two-stage Type-A partial interference, and RigdonHudgens2015 constructs exact confidence sets for those binary two-stage effects. Neither treats this unequal-clique Bernoulli All Treat versus All Control minimax expected-length problem or proves the open water-filling lower frontier. AronowSamii2017 supplies the design--exposure--estimand architecture and exposure-specific inverse weighting, while UganderKarrerBackstromKleinberg2013 shows that full-neighborhood exposure probabilities may be exponentially small in degree. BasseAiroldi2018 gives a nonconcentration warning, UganderYin2023 changes the design to mitigate small exposure probabilities, and KandirosHarshawSavje2026 studies design-based mean-squared-error criteria rather than all-interval confidence length. CaiLow2004 and ArmstrongKolesar2018 motivate modulus arguments in Gaussian experiments, but do not provide the heterogeneous weighted-erasure interval-spread theorem required here. The common-location construction is used only for the proved cubic consistency lower bound, and the product-Rademacher argument is confined to the specified two-scale family.
prose_updates.interpretation: The computable quantity \(\rho_0(w,q)\), equivalently the unit-budget capped modulus \(\omega_1(w,q)\), is the intrinsic consistency diagnostic. A rare block may keep \(S\) bounded away from zero while carrying so little causal weight that trimming it still permits vanishing honest length. At nonzero finite confidence, the corrected trimmed interval has risk at most five times the capped modulus, while the general converse is presently cubic. The sharper \(k^{-1/2}\) lower rate is proved only for the explicit two-scale family and does not settle the universal linear frontier.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The common-location no-reveal construction yields \(\mathcal R_\alpha\gtrsim\omega_\alpha^3/\log(1/\alpha)\), which is sufficient for the fixed-confidence consistency equivalence but can be much smaller than \(\omega_\alpha\). The unrestricted sharp lower bound and the no-dominance sharp lower half therefore remain open forms of the same universal linear weighted-erasure interval-spread problem. A resolution must control compact-support boundaries, random weighted reveal information, conditional target fluctuation, and external interval randomization; neither the exact embedding, the cubic argument, nor the family-specific product-Rademacher lemma supplies that universal step.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The proved results concern fixed outcomes in \([-1/2,1/2]\), known unequal disjoint clique blocks, and independent unit-level \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) assignment. The estimator and upper intervals are measurable from \(D\) and known design quantities. The capped optimizer, factor-\(5/2\) trimming comparison, factor-five unrestricted upper bound, exact consistency boundary, and cubic lower bound cover arbitrary independent external interval randomization. The fixed-confidence \(\Theta_\alpha(k^{-1/2})\) statement is confined to the specified two-scale family; it is not a universal posterior-spread theorem. The equal-block and general no-dominance results retain only their proved upper conclusions. Overlapping or nonclique neighborhoods are rejected before the software diagnostic reports an interval.

statement_notes.justification: The capped optimizer, trimming dual, unrestricted upper bound, no-cap formula, and exact consistency boundary are proved; this question is retained solely for the matching all-measurable randomized-interval lower bound.
statement_notes.gap: Only the universal linear relation \(\mathcal R_\alpha\gtrsim\min\{1,\omega_\alpha\}\) remains open; the optimizer, duality, upper bound, and zero-versus-nonzero boundary are no longer part of the gap.
statement_notes.consumer: Closing this question would add a two-sided sharp expected-length rate without changing the already-proved consistency boundary.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a block \(B_l\).  By
\(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}bernoulli}\), each of its
\(2^{r_l}\) assignment vectors has probability \(2^{-r_l}=q_l\).
Exactly one vector is all treated and exactly one is all controlled.
Thus
\[
 P_Z(A_l=1)=q_l,\qquad P_Z(C_l=1)=q_l,
 \qquad P_Z(H_l=1)=1-2q_l,
\tag{1}
\]
and \(A_lC_l=0\) on every assignment.  By
\(\mathrm{ass{:}partition}\), distinct triples
\((A_l,C_l,H_l)\) depend on disjoint coordinates of \(Z\); their
independence therefore follows from
\(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}bernoulli}\).

Put \(u_l=\mu_l(a)\) and \(v_l=\mu_l(b)\).  The fixed-schedule and
bounded-outcome assumptions, together with
\(\mathrm{def{:}block\text{-}means}\), give
\[
 -\frac12\le u_l,v_l\le\frac12.
\tag{2}
\]
On the all-treated and all-control events,
\(\mathrm{lem{:}observed\text{-}block\text{-}means}\) identifies the
observed block mean with \(u_l\) and \(v_l\), respectively.  Mutual
exclusion then rewrites the observed statistic, on every assignment,
as
\[
 X_l=\frac{w_l}{q_l}(A_lu_l-C_lv_l).
\tag{3}
\]
Using (1), fixedness of \((u_l,v_l)\), and \(A_lC_l=0\),
\[
 \mathbb E_ZX_l=w_l(u_l-v_l),
\tag{4}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Var}_Z(X_l)
 &\le \mathbb E_ZX_l^2\\
 &=\frac{w_l^2}{q_l}(u_l^2+v_l^2)\\
 &\le\frac{w_l^2}{2q_l},
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]
where the last step uses (2).  Summing (5) and using the definition of
\(S\) proves
\[
 \sum_{l=1}^L\operatorname{Var}_Z(X_l)
 \le\frac12\sum_{l=1}^L\frac{w_l^2}{q_l}=\frac S2.
\tag{6}
\]

It remains to compute the exact centered increment.  Write
\(W_l=X_l-\mathbb E_ZX_l\).  Equations (3)--(4) give the following
three exhaustive cases:
\[
 \frac{W_l}{w_l}=
 \begin{cases}
  (q_l^{-1}-1)u_l+v_l,&A_l=1,\\
  -u_l-(q_l^{-1}-1)v_l,&C_l=1,\\
  -u_l+v_l,&H_l=1.
 \end{cases}
\tag{7}
\]
Since \(r_l\ge1\), one has \(0<q_l\le1/2\), so all coefficients
whose absolute values are summed below are nonnegative.  By (2), the
first two rows of (7) have absolute value at most
\[
 \frac12(q_l^{-1}-1)+\frac12=\frac1{2q_l}.
\tag{8}
\]
The third row has absolute value at most one, which is at most
\(1/(2q_l)\) because \(q_l\le1/2\).  Hence on every assignment
\[
 |X_l-mathbb E_ZX_l|=|W_l|
 \le\frac{w_l}{2q_l}\le\frac M2.
\tag{9}
\]
This is an enumeration of All Treat, All Control, and every other
assignment, rather than a triangle bound on \(|X_l|+|\mathbb EX_l|\).

For the smallest unequal stress test, take a singleton block and a
two-unit block.  Their \(2\cdot4=8\) joint assignments give categorical
counts \((1,1,0)\) and \((1,1,2)\), respectively.  Substitution in
(7), for arbitrary endpoints \(u_l,v_l\in[-1/2,1/2]\), verifies (8)
and (9) on each of the eight assignments; thus the asserted support,
mean, variance, and increment formulas also hold exactly at this
finite boundary case.

Fix \(m\in\mathcal M_n(B)\), and define
\[
 W_l=X_l-mathbb E_ZX_l,qquad z=\log(2/\alpha)>0.
\tag{10}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}block\text{-}reduction}\), the variables \(W_l\)
are independent and centered and obey
\[
 v:=\sum_{l=1}^L\mathbb E_ZW_l^2\le\frac S2,
 \qquad |W_l|\le\frac M2.
\tag{11}
\]
Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}finite\text{-}product\text{-}exponential}\)
with \(c=M/2\) and the value of \(z\) in (10).  Because its threshold
is nondecreasing in \(v\), (11) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_Z\!\left\{\left|\sum_{l=1}^LW_l\right|>
 \sqrt{S\log(2/\alpha)}
 +\frac M6\log(2/\alpha)\right\}
 &\le 2\exp\{-\log(2/\alpha)\}\\
 &=\alpha.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
The expectation identity in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}block\text{-}reduction}\), followed by the definition
of the causal estimand, yields
\[
 \sum_{l=1}^L\mathbb E_ZX_l
 =\sum_{l=1}^Lw_l\{\mu_l(a)-\mu_l(b)\}=\theta.
\tag{13}
\]
Since \(\widehat\theta=\sum_lX_l\) by
\(\mathrm{def{:}block\text{-}ht}\), equations (12)--(13) and the
corrected construction in \(\mathrm{def{:}clipped\text{-}ht}\) imply
\[
 P_{Z,m}\{|\widehat\theta-  heta|\le h_\alpha\}
 \ge1-\alpha.
\tag{14}
\]

Every \(X_l\), and hence \(\widehat\theta\), is measurable from
\(D\) by \(\mathrm{def{:}block\text{-}ht}\) and
\(\mathrm{lem{:}observed\text{-}block\text{-}means}\).  The quantities
\(S\), \(M\), and \(\alpha\) are known design inputs.  Moreover,
bounded outcomes give
\(\mu_l(a)-\mu_l(b)\in[-1,1]\), and membership in
\(\mathcal M_n(B)\), through its partition condition and the
definition \(w_l=r_l/n\), gives \(\sum_lw_l=1\).  Thus
\(\theta\in[-1,1]\).  On the event in (14), intersecting the raw
interval with \([-1,1]\) cannot remove \(\theta\), proving
\[
 P_{Z,m}\{\theta\in I_{\mathrm{HT},\alpha}(D)\}\ge1-\alpha.
\tag{15}
\]
Finally, the length of an intersection is at most the length of each
of the two intersected intervals, whence, pointwise in \(D\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{len}\{I_{\mathrm{HT},\alpha}(D)\}
 &\le\min\{2,2h_\alpha\}\\
 &=2\min\!\left\{1,\sqrt{S\log(2/\alpha)}
       +\frac M6\log(2/\alpha)\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]
This is a deterministic finite-sample length certificate, so it also
holds for every assignment in the exhaustive unequal three-unit
stress test of \(\mathrm{lem{:}block\text{-}reduction}\).

Put \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\) and \(y=\log(2/\alpha)\).  Since
\(0<\alpha\le1/4\), one has \(x\ge\log4\), and hence
\[
 y=x+\log2\le\frac32x.
\tag{17}
\]
The corrected \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}upper}\) supplies a
deterministic observed-data interval that is honest uniformly over
\(\mathcal M_n(B)\) and has pointwise length at most
\[
 2\min\left\{1,\sqrt{Sy}+\frac{My}{6}\right\}.
\tag{18}
\]
It is therefore an admissible deterministic member of
\(\mathfrak C_\alpha\).  Although
\(\mathrm{def{:}length\text{-}risk}\) also permits procedures using
the independent randomizer \(R\), taking the infimum over the larger
class cannot invalidate the upper bound furnished by this one rule.
Thus (18) bounds \(\mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)\).

Take \(c_0=1\).  Under the no-dominance hypothesis
\(M\sqrt{x}\le\sqrt S\), equation (17) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sqrt{Sy}+\frac{My}{6}
 &\le\sqrt{\frac32}\sqrt{Sx}+\frac14Mx\\
 &\le\left(\sqrt{\frac32}+\frac14\right)\sqrt{Sx}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]
For every \(K\ge1\) and \(t\ge0\),
\(\min\{1,Kt\}\le K\min\{1,t\}\).  Since
\(K=\sqrt{3/2}+1/4>1\), equations (18)--(19) prove
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le C_1\min\{1,\sqrt{S\log(1/\alpha)}\},
 \qquad
 C_1=2\left(\sqrt{\frac32}+\frac14\right).
\tag{20}
\]
Both \(c_0\) and \(C_1\) are universal, as required.

The total population size is \(2k+4k=6k\).  Hence a size-two block has
\[
 w_l=\frac2{6k}=\frac1{3k},\qquad q_l=2^{-2}=\frac14,
\]
whereas a size-four block has
\[
 w_l=\frac4{6k}=\frac2{3k},\qquad q_l=2^{-4}=\frac1{16}.
\]
The reveal probabilities follow directly from
\(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}bernoulli}\).  Substitution into the
definitions of \(S\) and \(M\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 S
 &=k\frac{(1/(3k))^2}{1/4}
   +k\frac{(2/(3k))^2}{1/16}
   =\frac4{9k}+\frac{64}{9k}
   =\frac{68}{9k},\\
 M
 &=\max\left\{\frac{1/(3k)}{1/4},
                \frac{2/(3k)}{1/16}\right\}
   =\frac{32}{3k}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{35}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \frac{M\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}}{\sqrt S}
 =\frac{32\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}}{\sqrt{68k}}
 \longrightarrow0
\tag{36}
\]
for every fixed \(0<\alpha\le1/4\).  The hypothesis of
\(\mathrm{thm{:}no\text{-}dominance\text{-}upper}\) therefore holds
for all sufficiently large \(k\).  For such \(k\), the square-root
term is also below one, and that theorem plus (35) yields
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le C_1\sqrt{\frac{68\log(1/\alpha)}{9k}}.
\tag{37}
\]
For \(k\ge64\),
\(\mathrm{lem{:}two\text{-}scale\text{-}rademacher\text{-}lower}\)
gives
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)\ge\frac1{192\sqrt{k}}.
\tag{38}
\]
Equations (37)--(38) prove
\(\mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)=\Theta_\alpha(k^{-1/2})\) at every fixed
confidence level in the stated range.  The lower bound invoked here is
specialized to the \(k\) size-two blocks and makes no assertion about
either universal weighted-erasure lower open question.

Finally, the cap breakpoints in
\(\mathrm{def{:}capped\text{-}modulus}\) are \(q_l/w_l\).  They are
\[
 \frac{1/4}{1/(3k)}=\frac{3k}{4},
 \qquad
 \frac{1/16}{2/(3k)}=\frac{3k}{32}.
\tag{39}
\]
Since \(r\mapsto2^{-r}\) is injective on the positive integers, one
common block size cannot reproduce both reveal probabilities.  The
two distinct values in (39) likewise rule out a common breakpoint.

added_lemmas.statement:
For the family \(B^{(k)}\) containing \(k\) blocks of size two and \(k\) blocks of size four, every \(0<\alpha\le 1/4\) and every integer \(k\ge64\) satisfy
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)\ge \frac{1}{192\sqrt{k}}.
\]
This lower bound applies to the full class of measurable honest interval procedures, including procedures externally randomized by \(R\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), an integer \(k\ge64\), and an arbitrary
\(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\).  Index the \(k\) size-two blocks by
\(j=1,\ldots,k\).  In the hard schedules from
\(\mathrm{def{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\), put
\[
 V_j=\frac{\varepsilon_j}{2},\qquad
 P(\varepsilon_j=1)=P(\varepsilon_j=-1)=\frac12
 \quad(j=1,\ldots,k),
\tag{21}
\]
independently, and set \(V_l=1/2\) deterministically on every
size-four block.  This product law is used only to average the
pointwise coverage and risk inequalities furnished by
\(\mathrm{lem{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\); every
schedule in its support is a fixed member of
\(\mathcal M_n(B^{(k)})\).  For a size-two block,
\[
 q_j=\frac14,qquad w_j=\frac1{3k}.
\tag{22}
\]
Let \(K_j\) be its all-treated reveal indicator and define
\[
 N=\sum_{j=1}^k(1-K_j).
\tag{23}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\),
the \(K_j\) are independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/4)\)
variables, independent of the signs in (21).  Consequently
\[
 N\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(k,3/4),\qquad
 \mathbb EN=\frac{3k}{4},\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(N)=\frac{3k}{16}.
\tag{24}
\]

Write \(\Lambda=\Lambda_\Gamma(O,R)\) for the randomized interval in
the erasure experiment constructed in
\(\mathrm{def{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\), and
put \(L_\Lambda=\operatorname{len}(\Lambda)\).  Conditional on
\((O,R)\), the revealed size-two signs and the size-four contribution
are fixed, while the \(N\) unrevealed size-two signs remain independent
fair Rademacher variables.  Indeed, \(O\) contains only
\((K_j,K_jV_j)\), and the external \(R\) is independent of the
assignment and prior signs.  Since \(\theta=\sum_lw_lV_l\) on these
schedules, its conditional law has the form
\[
 c(O)+\frac1{6k}\sum_{s=1}^{N}\xi_s,
\tag{25}
\]
where the \(\xi_s\) are conditionally independent fair Rademacher
variables.  Adjacent support points in (25) are separated by
\(1/(3k)\).

We prove the atom bound used below.  For
\(S_N=\sum_{s=1}^N\xi_s\), its largest atom is
\[
 p_N=2^{-N}\binom{N}{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}.
\]
If \(N=2m\), factorial cancellation gives
\[
 p_{2m}=4^{-m}\binom{2m}{m}
       =\prod_{s=1}^m\left(1-\frac1{2s}\right).
\]
The inequalities \(\log(1-u)\le-u\) for \(0<u<1\) and
\(\sum_{s=1}^m s^{-1}\ge\int_1^{m+1}t^{-1}\,dt=\log(m+1)\) imply
\[
 p_{2m}\le(m+1)^{-1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac2{2m}}.
\tag{26}
\]
If \(N=2m+1\), then
\[
 p_{2m+1}=\frac{2m+1}{2m+2}p_{2m}
 \le(m+1)^{-1/2}
 \le\sqrt{\frac2{2m+1}}.
\tag{27}
\]
The case \(N=1\) also satisfies (27), so for every \(N\ge1\),
\[
 p_N\le\sqrt{\frac2N}.
\tag{28}
\]

An interval of length \(u\) contains at most \(3ku+1\) points of a
lattice having spacing \(1/(3k)\).  It follows from (25) and (28) that
on \(N\ge k/2\), conditionally on \((O,R)\),
\[
 P\{\theta\in\Lambda\mid O,R\}
 \le(3kL_\Lambda+1)\sqrt{\frac2N}.
\tag{29}
\]
In particular, on
\[
 \mathcal A=\left\{N\ge\frac k2,\quad
 L_\Lambda<\frac1{48\sqrt{k}}\right\},
\]
equation (29) and \(k\ge64\) give
\[
 P\{\theta\in\Lambda\mid O,R\}
 \le\left(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{16}+1\right)\frac2{\sqrt{k}}
 =\frac18+\frac2{\sqrt{k}}
 \le\frac38.
\tag{30}
\]
On \(N<k/2\), equation (24) gives
\(|N-\mathbb EN|>k/4\).  Markov's inequality applied to
\((N-\mathbb EN)^2\), followed by (24), yields
\[
 P\left(N<\frac k2\right)
 \le\frac{3k/16}{(k/4)^2}
 =\frac3k\le\frac3{64}.
\tag{31}
\]

Pointwise honesty of \(\Gamma\), averaged over the product law (21),
and the coverage identity in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\) imply
\[
 P\{\theta\in\Lambda\}\ge1-\alpha\ge\frac34.
\tag{32}
\]
On \(\mathcal A\), conditional coverage is at most \(3/8\) by (30),
and outside \(\mathcal A\) it is at most one.  The complement of
\(\mathcal A\) is contained in the union of
\(\{N<k/2\}\) and
\(\{L_\Lambda\ge1/(48\sqrt{k})\}\).  Hence
\[
 \frac34
 \le P\{\theta\in\Lambda\}
 \le\frac38+P\left(N<\frac k2\right)
      +P\left(L_\Lambda\ge\frac1{48\sqrt{k}}\right).
\]
Using (31),
\[
 P\left(L_\Lambda\ge\frac1{48\sqrt{k}}\right)
 \ge\frac38-\frac3{64}=\frac{21}{64}\ge\frac14.
\tag{33}
\]
Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E L_\Lambda
 \ge\frac1{48\sqrt{k}}
 P\left(L_\Lambda\ge\frac1{48\sqrt{k}}\right)
 \ge\frac1{192\sqrt{k}}.
\tag{34}
\]
The expected-length identity and supremum inequality in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}hard\text{-}subexperiment\text{-}embedding}\) show
that the worst fixed-schedule risk of the original \(\Gamma\) is at
least the product-prior average in (34).  Since \(\Gamma\) was an
arbitrary member of \(\mathfrak C_\alpha\), taking the infimum in
\(\mathrm{def{:}length\text{-}risk}\) proves the claimed inequality.
The construction conditions throughout on the declared independent
coordinate \(R\), so it covers every externally randomized measurable
interval in the decision class.

added_lemmas.gap: The argument is deliberately specialized to this two-scale family and does not settle either universal linear lower-bound open question.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
Let \(B^{(k)}\) contain \(k\) blocks of size two and \(k\) blocks of
size four, so \(n=6k\).  The two strata have
\((w_l,q_l)=(1/(3k),1/4)\) and
\((w_l,q_l)=(2/(3k),1/16)\), respectively, and
\[
 S=\frac{68}{9k},\qquad M=\frac{32}{3k},\qquad
 \frac{M\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}}{\sqrt S}
 =\frac{32\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}}{\sqrt{68k}}.
\]
Thus, for every fixed \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), the no-dominance condition
holds for all sufficiently large \(k\).  With \(C_1\) denoting the
universal constant in
\(\mathrm{thm{:}no\text{-}dominance\text{-}upper}\), for every
sufficiently large \(k\),
\[
 \frac{1}{192\sqrt{k}}
 \le \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le C_1\sqrt{\frac{68\log(1/\alpha)}{9k}},
\]
and consequently \(\mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)=\Theta_\alpha(k^{-1/2})\).
The two water-filling breakpoints \(q_l/w_l\) are \(3k/4\) and
\(3k/32\).  No common block size can reproduce both reveal
probabilities, or both breakpoints.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: On the fixed-confidence asymptotic regime, the specialized product-Rademacher lemma supplies the missing lower half, so the concrete family can state the directed two-sided order without asserting a universal erasure lower bound.

proposed_definition_changes.reason: Exact enumeration gives the centered block increment bound \(w_l/(2q_l)\le M/2\); Bernstein's linear term is therefore \(M\log(2/\alpha)/6\).

proposed_definition_changes.proposed: \(\rho_\alpha(w,q)=\inf_{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}}[\sum_{l\notin J}w_l+\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)\sum_{l\in J}w_l^2/q_l}+\{\log(2/\alpha)/6\}\max_{l\in J}w_l/q_l]\), with the maximum over \(J=\varnothing\) equal to zero, and \(\rho_0(w,q)=\inf_J[\sum_{l\notin J}w_l+(\sum_{l\in J}w_l^2/q_l)^{1/2}]\).
proposed_definition_changes.reason: The same exact centered-increment calculation on every retained subset \(J\) changes the trimmed Bernstein term from \(M_J\log(2/\alpha)/3\) to \(M_J\log(2/\alpha)/6\).

proofs.proof_tex:
Because every block is nonempty, \(w_l>0\); and because
\(q_l=2^{-r_l}\), also \(q_l>0\).  For \(z>0\), define
\[
 \mathcal D_z=\left\{\delta\in[0,1]^L:
                 \sum_{l=1}^Lq_l\delta_l^2\le z\right\}.
\tag{1}
\]
This is a nonempty compact subset of \(\mathbb R^L\), and the linear
objective is continuous, so a maximizer exists.  If
\(z\ge\sum_lq_l\), then \((1,\ldots,1)\in\mathcal D_z\); it is optimal
because \(w_l>0\) and every feasible coordinate is at most one.

Suppose henceforth that \(0<z<\sum_lq_l\).  The function
\[
 f(\lambda)=\sum_{l=1}^Lq_l
       \min\{1,\lambda w_l/q_l\}^2,
 \qquad \lambda\ge0,
\tag{2}
\]
is continuous, equals zero at zero, and is strictly increasing until
all coordinates reach their caps, after which it equals
\(\sum_lq_l\).  The intermediate value theorem therefore gives a
unique \(\lambda>0\), before the terminal plateau, such that
\(f(\lambda)=z\).  Put
\[
 \delta_l^*=\min\{1,\lambda w_l/q_l\}.
\tag{3}
\]
This vector belongs to \(\mathcal D_z\) and makes its quadratic
constraint active.

To certify optimality, let \(C=\{l:\delta_l^*=1\}\), let
\(J=C^c\), and take any \(\delta\in\mathcal D_z\).  For \(l\in J\),
the identity \(w_l=q_l\delta_l^*/\lambda\) and the inequality
\((\delta_l-\delta_l^*)^2\ge0\) give
\[
 w_l(\delta_l-\delta_l^*)
 \le \frac{q_l}{2\lambda}
       \{\delta_l^2-(\delta_l^*)^2\}.
\tag{4}
\]
For \(l\in C\), the cap relation gives \(w_l\ge q_l/\lambda\).
Because \(\delta_l-1\le0\) and \((\delta_l-1)^2\ge0\),
\[
 w_l(\delta_l-1)
 \le\frac{q_l}{\lambda}(\delta_l-1)
 \le\frac{q_l}{2\lambda}(\delta_l^2-1).
\tag{5}
\]
Summing (4)--(5), using feasibility of \(\delta\), and using the active
constraint for \(\delta^*\), yields
\[
 \sum_{l=1}^Lw_l(\delta_l-\delta_l^*)
 \le\frac1{2\lambda}
       \sum_{l=1}^Lq_l\{\delta_l^2-(\delta_l^*)^2\}
 \le0.
\tag{6}
\]
Thus (3) is the global optimizer.  Equations (4)--(6) are also a
first-order optimality certificate for the capped convex feasible
program.

We now compare the two moduli.  Fix a vector \(\delta\) feasible for
the capped program at budget \(x\), and fix
\(J_0\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}\).  Since \(0\le\delta_l\le1\),
Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{l=1}^Lw_l\delta_l
 &\le \sum_{l\notin J_0}w_l+
      \sum_{l\in J_0}w_l\delta_l\\
 &\le \sum_{l\notin J_0}w_l+
 \left(\sum_{l\in J_0}\frac{w_l^2}{q_l}\right)^{1/2}
 \left(\sum_{l\in J_0}q_l\delta_l^2\right)^{1/2}\\
 &\le \sum_{l\notin J_0}w_l+
 \sqrt{x\sum_{l\in J_0}w_l^2/q_l}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
The corrected construction of \(\rho_\alpha\) has the larger square-root
coefficient \(\sqrt y\), because \(y=x+\log2\ge x\), and has a
nonnegative linear term.  Taking the supremum over feasible \(\delta\)
and then the infimum over \(J_0\) in (7) proves
\[
 \omega_\alpha(w,q)\le\rho_\alpha(w,q).
\tag{8}
\]

If \(x\ge\sum_lq_l\), the optimizer is all-capped and
\(\omega_\alpha=\sum_lw_l=1\).  Choosing \(J_0=\varnothing\) gives
\(\rho_\alpha\le1=\omega_\alpha\).  It remains to treat
\(x<\sum_lq_l\).  Apply (3) at budget \(x\), retain its capped set
\(C\) and uncapped set \(J\), and define
\[
 A=\sum_{l\in J}\frac{w_l^2}{q_l},\qquad
 Q_C=\sum_{l\in C}q_l,
 \qquad B=\sum_{l\in C}w_l.
\tag{9}
\]
The active constraint and the objective value are
\[
 x=Q_C+\lambda^2A,
 \qquad
 \omega_\alpha=B+\lambda A.
\tag{10}
\]
For \(l\in C\), \(\lambda w_l/q_l\ge1\), so
\(B\ge Q_C/\lambda\).  For \(l\in J\),
\(w_l/q_l<1/\lambda\).  Consequently (10) implies
\[
 \omega_\alpha\ge\frac{x}{\lambda},
 \qquad A\le\frac{x}{\lambda^2},
 \qquad \max_{l\in J}\frac{w_l}{q_l}<\frac1\lambda.
\tag{11}
\]
Because \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), \(x\ge\log4=2\log2\), and hence
\(y=x+\log2\le3x/2\).  Choosing \(J_0=J\) in the corrected definition,
whose linear coefficient is \(y/6\), and applying (10)--(11), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \rho_\alpha
 &\le B+\sqrt{yA}
       +\frac y6\max_{l\in J}\frac{w_l}{q_l}\\
 &\le B+\sqrt{\frac32}\,\frac{x}{\lambda}
       +\frac14\frac{x}{\lambda}\\
 &\le\left(1+\sqrt{\frac32}+\frac14\right)\omega_\alpha
 <\frac52\omega_\alpha.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
Together with the all-capped case, this proves the confidence-level
comparison.

Finally, repeat (7) with quadratic budget one and without the linear
term to obtain \(\omega_1\le\rho_0\).  If
\(\sum_lq_l\le1\), the budget-one optimizer is all-capped, so choosing
the empty retained set yields
\[
 \rho_0\le1=\omega_1.
\tag{13}
\]
If \(\sum_lq_l>1\), apply (9)--(11) with \(x=1\).  Choosing the
uncapped set in the definition of \(\rho_0\) gives
\[
 \rho_0\le B+\sqrt A
 \le B+\lambda^{-1}
 \le2\omega_1.
\tag{14}
\]
Equations (13)--(14) establish
\(\omega_1\le\rho_0\le2\omega_1\), completing the proof.

Fix \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), put \(x=\log(1/\alpha)>1\), and, for this
proof, write
\[
 \omega_z(w,q)=
 \max\left\{\sum_{l=1}^Lw_l\delta_l:
 0\le\delta_l\le1,\ 
 \sum_{l=1}^Lq_l\delta_l^2\le z\right\}.
\tag{17}
\]
Thus \(\omega_\alpha=\omega_x\), whereas \(\omega_1\) is the
budget-one modulus in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\).  Since
\(x>1\), nesting of the feasible sets gives \(\omega_1\le\omega_x\).
Conversely, if \(\delta\) is feasible at budget \(x\), then
\(\delta/\sqrt{x}\in[0,1]^L\) and
\[
 \sum_{l=1}^Lq_l(\delta_l/\sqrt{x})^2\le1.
\]
The objective at \(\delta/\sqrt{x}\) is the objective at \(\delta\)
divided by \(\sqrt{x}\).  Taking suprema therefore proves
\[
 \omega_1\le\omega_\alpha\le\sqrt{x}\,\omega_1.
\tag{18}
\]
By the budget-one comparison in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\),
\[
 \omega_1\le\rho_0\le2\omega_1.
\tag{19}
\]
Because \(x\) is fixed along the triangular array, (18)--(19) imply
\[
 \omega_\alpha\to0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \rho_0\to0.
\tag{20}
\]

The unrestricted upper bound
\(\mathrm{prop{:}unrestricted\text{-}water\text{-}filling\text{-}upper}\)
gives
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le5\min\{1,\omega_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\tag{21}
\]
Thus \(\omega_\alpha\to0\) implies \(\mathcal R_\alpha\to0\).  In the
opposite direction, the established all-procedure lower bound
\(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}erasure\text{-}consistency\text{-}lower}\)
states, row by row, that
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \ge\frac{\omega_\alpha(w,q)^3}{136x}.
\tag{22}
\]
The fixed number \(136x\) is finite and positive.  Hence
\(\mathcal R_\alpha\to0\) forces \(\omega_\alpha^3\to0\), and therefore
\(\omega_\alpha\to0\).  Combining (20)--(22) proves the three-way
equivalence.

For sufficiency of \(S^{(n)}\to0\), let \(\delta\) be feasible at
budget \(x\).  Positivity of each \(q_l\) permits division by
\(\sqrt{q_l}\), and Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{l=1}^Lw_l\delta_l
 &=\sum_{l=1}^L\frac{w_l}{\sqrt{q_l}}
                    \sqrt{q_l}\delta_l\\
 &\le
 \left(\sum_{l=1}^L\frac{w_l^2}{q_l}\right)^{1/2}
 \left(\sum_{l=1}^Lq_l\delta_l^2\right)^{1/2}
 \le\sqrt{xS}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{23}
\]
Maximizing the left side proves
\(\omega_\alpha\le\sqrt{xS}\).  Since \(x\) is fixed, (21) now shows
that \(S^{(n)}\to0\) implies \(\mathcal R_\alpha\to0\).

It remains to prove nonnecessity.  For each integer \(k\ge1\), set
\(n_k=2k\,2^k\).  Partition the \(n_k\) units into one block of size
\(2k\) and \(n_k-2k\) singleton blocks.  These are nonempty, disjoint,
and exhaust the population, so the construction obeys
\(\mathrm{ass{:}partition}\).  Under
\(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}bernoulli}\), the large block has
\[
 w_{\mathrm{big}}=\frac{2k}{n_k}=2^{-k},
 \qquad q_{\mathrm{big}}=2^{-2k},
 \qquad
 \frac{w_{\mathrm{big}}^2}{q_{\mathrm{big}}}=1.
\tag{24}
\]
Every singleton block has \(w_l=1/n_k\) and \(q_l=1/2\).  It follows
directly from the definition of \(S\) that
\[
 S^{(n_k)}
 =1+\frac{2(n_k-2k)}{n_k^2}
 \longrightarrow1,
\tag{25}
\]
so this sequence does not have \(S^{(n_k)}\to0\).

Let \(J_k\) consist of all singleton blocks, and put
\(y=\log(2/\alpha)\).  The omitted weight is \(2^{-k}\), the retained
quadratic sum is \(2(n_k-2k)/n_k^2\), and the largest retained ratio
\(w_l/q_l\) is \(2/n_k\).  Substitution in the corrected trimmed
radius, whose linear coefficient is \(y/6\), gives
\[
 \rho_\alpha(w^{(n_k)},q^{(n_k)})
 \le2^{-k}
 +\sqrt{\frac{2y(n_k-2k)}{n_k^2}}
 +\frac{y}{3n_k}
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{26}
\]
By (8), \(\omega_\alpha\le\rho_\alpha\), so (26) and (21) imply
\(\mathcal R_\alpha(w^{(n_k)},q^{(n_k)})\to0\).  Together with (25),
this is an explicit unequal-clique triangular array proving that
\(S^{(n)}\to0\) is not necessary.

added_lemmas.proof_tex:
By \(\mathrm{thm{:}trimmed\text{-}upper}\), there is an interval in
\(\mathfrak C_\alpha\) having pointwise length at most
\(2\min\{1,\rho_\alpha(w,q)\}\).  The definition of minimax risk
therefore gives
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le2\min\{1,\rho_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\tag{15}
\]
The strengthened comparison in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\) and
monotonicity of \(u\mapsto\min\{1,u\}\) imply
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le2\min\left\{1,\frac52\omega_\alpha(w,q)\right\}
 \le5\min\{1,\omega_\alpha(w,q)\}.
\tag{16}
\]
The last inequality follows by considering
\(\omega_\alpha\le1\) and \(\omega_\alpha>1\) separately.  This proves
the unrestricted upper bound.
